#296. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.

New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

#295. Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

#292. Joshua Kimmich critcizes Bayern bosses over Musiala health comments

Joshua Kimmich has slammed Bayern Munich's leadership over comments about Jamal Musiala's health issues. The bosses have questioned whether the player can return to previous form – and is still worth his high salary.

Bayern Munich's disappointing 2-1 Champions League defeat at Lille on Wednesday night – in which Jamal Musiala came on for the last quarter of an hour – was overshadowed by comments the club's captain made afterwards.

"It must never happen that something like this is played out at a player's expense. Of course, the club always comes first and is bigger than the player, but it's not bigger than the person," Kimmich told reporters in the mixed zone.

"That's an absolute no-go and not Bayern-like," he added.

Kimmich was responding to recent comments made by Bayern supervisory board members Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge.

"If he (Musiala) doesn't return to being the Jamal of old, then we need to have a conversation with his family, with the player, and, above all, with his agency – because, frankly, the current financial figures would no longer be justifiable," Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told Sky on Friday.

Honorary President Uli Hoeness has described the situation as a "dilemma" for the club, while CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen raised the prospect of talks with Musiala's management and family.

While theGermany player has struggled with a number of injuries over the past couple of seasons, his health came into sharper focus in August, after he collapsed on the pitch in a couple of preseason matches. He subsequently revealed that he had been diagnosed with a neurological condition which causes him to suffer from occasional "absence seizures."

Kimmich added that criticism of a players' performances was legitimate, but that concerns about Musiala's situation should have been dealt with behind closed doors.

"That's something you should sort out internally, around a table, rather than trying to resolve it publicly," he said.

"It's not that he has problems because he's unprofessional. He's there every day trying to get the maximum out of himself."

Meanwhile, Bayern bosses met with Musiala's agents on Tuesday, and clarified the timeline of events, dismissing speculation that the player could have concealed the condition when he signed his last contract extension.

Bayern said the two sides agreed that he was first examined for seizure symptoms in April 2025, two months after he had signed his contract extension, which makes him one of the club's top earners and is to keep him in Munich until 2030. Discussions between Bayern management and Musiala's representatives are reportedly ongoing.

#290. AI is straining America’s open records systems

Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#287. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”

#285. How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation.

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

#283. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#282. EU-Indonesia trade deal opens new markets, but challenges remain

The agreement offers new export and investment opportunities for Jakarta and Brussels. But can Indonesia turn Europe's growing interest in its markets and critical minerals into sustainable gains at home?

As the European Union seeks to deepen its presence in Asia and diversify its trade relationships, Indonesia is emerging as an increasingly important partner.

At a signing ceremony in Brussels last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the bloc's trade agreement with Jakarta as one of its "most ambitious deals" in the region, linking markets of 730 million people.

The deal, the culmination of nearly a decade of negotiations, reflects the EU's efforts to diversify its trade partnerships, secure access to critical raw materials and reduce strategic dependencies on China.

For Indonesia, it offers opportunities to attract investment, expand exports and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

The agreement will gradually scrap tariffs on more than 98% of product categories, covering almost the entire value of bilateral trade over 15 years.

For the EU, gaining better access to critical raw materials, particularly nickel, and diversifying its supply chains are central to its strategic partnership with Indonesia, said Philip Schleifer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Amsterdam.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The main strategic interests are opening up a large and growing market for European companies, diversifying and deepening its economic partnerships, reducing strategic dependencies on China, and securing access to critical raw materials," Schleifer told DW.

Indonesia's mineral resources are particularly important for Europe's green and digital transitions. Nickel, for instance, is a key material for batteries and electric vehicles.

The agreement also creates opportunities for European investment in strategic sectors, including electric vehicles, electronics and pharmaceuticals.

But Indonesia has its own industrial ambitions. The government wants to move beyond exporting raw materials by developing domestic processing industries and retaining more value from its natural resources.

"The challenge for the EU is to reconcile its own interest in securing raw material supply with Indonesia's industrial development objectives," said Eline Blot, a senior policy analyst at the Institute for European Environmental Policy (IEEP).

Yose Rizal Damuri, an economist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said his institution's study estimates Indonesian exports could increase by around 60% in the coming years.

"Not only can Indonesia increase exports to Europe, but it can also become more strongly integrated into the global supply chains of European companies," Yose told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Potential beneficiaries include labor-intensive manufacturing sectors such as textiles, garments, footwear and furniture, alongside other Indonesian commodities and manufactured products.

The agreement could also encourage European investment and create employment opportunities. However, Yose stressed that access to the European market does not automatically translate into higher exports.

He identified three priorities for Indonesia: raising awareness of the agreement among domestic businesses, strengthening production capacity and improving the country's business climate.

"Various trade agreements signed by Indonesia have relatively low utilization rates. The value of exports using these facilities remains limited compared with overall export values," he said, emphasizing the need for better information and outreach to producers.

Syafruddin Karimi, an economist at Andalas University in West Sumatra, also highlighted the opportunity to diversify Indonesia's export markets and reduce dependence on major trading partners such as China, the United States and regional Asian economies.

However, he warned that Indonesian producers must improve their compliance with European standards.

"Products must be traceable, including whether their production involves environmental damage or labor practices that undermine human dignity," Karimi said.

The expansion of trade and investment could also increase environmental pressures, particularly in nickel mining, palm oil production and manufacturing.

IEEP analyst Blot warned that increased production without stronger environmental safeguards could worsen pollution, ecosystem degradation and industrial emissions. "Nickel mining and processing can contribute to pollution and ecosystem degradation, while palm oil remains closely associated with deforestation," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU Deforestation Regulation presents another challenge for Indonesian producers, particularly small-scale farmers who may lack the resources, technical capacity and documentation needed to demonstrate compliance.

Blot acknowledged that these requirements could create disproportionate costs for smaller producers and potentially favor larger companies.

However, she cautioned against using smallholders' livelihoods as an argument to weaken environmental regulations.

"Rather than weakening environmental requirements, the priority should be to ensure that smallholders receive adequate financial and technical support to meet them," she said.

Schleifer at the University of Amsterdam also warned that growing global demand for Indonesian natural resources could create environmental and social problems previously associated with commodities such as timber, palm oil and coal.

While Indonesia has considerable bargaining power because of its mineral wealth, the challenge is ensuring that increased demand translates into domestic industrial development rather than simply expanding resource extraction.

The agreement includes a dedicated Trade and Sustainable Development chapter covering climate change, biodiversity conservation, sustainable forest management and labor rights. It also provides mechanisms for cooperation and civil society participation.

However, there is no guarantee these commitments will be implemented. "Experience with other EU trade agreements suggests that there is often a big gap between sustainability commitments on paper and outcomes on the ground," Schleifer said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Indonesia, the challenge also lies in preparing domestic industries to compete. Karimi stressed that the government, both at national and regional levels, must work with businesses to improve production standards, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises.

Yose also emphasized the importance of a predictable business environment, warning that frequent policy changes and regulatory uncertainty could discourage investors.

"Without improvements in the domestic business climate, this will not become a reality. Everything will remain good on paper but will not turn into real momentum for change," he said.

Ultimately, the trade agreement offers Indonesia an opportunity to strengthen its position in international trade and attract investment from Europe.

But whether the agreement delivers broader economic benefits will depend on the country's ability to develop competitive industries, move into higher-value production, and ensure that environmental protection and workers' rights are not overlooked.

DW's Muhammad Athif Aiman contributed to this article.

#281. The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

Avi Davidson is the first at-home user of an experimental prosthetic hand that lets him feel his wife’s hand in his own.

Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.

That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.

Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.

George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

The Black Friday deals have arrived! Set yourself up with a turkey sandwich and a warm drink, because it's time to shop the best sale event of the year. The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we highlight deals only on devices we’ve tested and would recommend to our own friends and family. Keychron is our favorite brand of keyboards, but they tend to be expensive. This is the best option in the lineup that’s actually quite affordable. Despite being cheaper, it still has a lot of the hallmarks of Keychron’s keyboards, including the hot-swappable switches, retro design, and high-end build quality. —Luke Larsen

There’s no mouse as beloved as Logitech’s MX Master line, primarily known for its comfortable grip, customization, and quality. The latest model makes a number of small tweaks to improve the mouse even further, including intuitive gesture controls and haptic feedback. If you take your work seriously, the MX Master 4 will be an excellent inclusion in your home office setup. —Luke Larsen

I’m still astounded that you can buy a high-quality 4K monitor for such little money these days. The Dell 27 Plus is my top pick as the monitor most people should buy, and the fact that it’s nearly $200 only bolsters that recommendation even more. The only compromise is that it’s a bit limited in terms of ports, but you can upgrade to the S2725DC with USB ports. —Luke Larsen

If you want an office chair that’s truly premium, the Steelcase Gesture is our recommendation. It’s a comfortable, attractive chair that comes in multiple colors, and you’ll find different sale prices for those different colors if you have a preference. It looks elegant, has a nice cushy seat, and you can adjust the lumbar support with the built-in tabs. —Nena Farrell

We’ve liked a few different Staples chairs over the years for a great office chair under $200, and while the Staples Dexley is our current pick (currently on sale too, but only $10 off), the Staples Hyken has a better deal. It’s down to $128, and it’s a good pick over the Dexley if you’re shorter. These seats both have great airflow and include a headrest. —Nena Farrell

Created from fabric scraps that would otherwise end up in a landfill, this thoughtfully constructed bag looks great and can carry everything you need for a weeklong trip. WIRED's Gear team has loved this bag for almost a decade now, and it's still one of our favorites. The pack straps and adjustable waist belt all tuck away neatly when you don't need them, turning this Allpa into more of a soft suitcase. —Scott Gilbertson

The Coraza is a gorgeous suitcase, and thanks to Cotopaxi's emphasis on ethical business, it's our top pick for the most sustainable carry on. Latched hard-shell luggage like the Coraza offers many of the benefits of an aluminum roller, but without the weight or the cost. If you want to upgrade your luggage without breaking the bank, the Coraza is a great choice. —Scott Gilbertson

Cotopaxi’s trim, colorful little bag swallows those odds and ends that would otherwise be careening around lose in your larger bag. It’s made from light recycled deadstock nylon and weighs in at a modest 6.5 ounces. The recycled fabric means your bag will be unique and the 4-liter capacity spread over three different compartments, gives you some organizational options. —Scott Gilbertson

Everything at Away Luggage is 25 percent off right now, including the Softside Carry-On, our top pick among roller bags. Multiple WIRED staffers own the hard-sided carry-on (currently $206 ($69 off) because it's good-looking and reasonably priced. However, former senior commerce editor Adrienne So prefers the brand's Softside Carry-On because it shows scuffs less easily, won't crack, and is more flexible if you overpack. —Scott Gilbertson

The Everywhere Tote is our favorite travel tote. Made from water-resistant nylon and accented with leather trim, I take the Everywhere Tote everywhere. It's the handbag you reach for when you're commuting, planning an overnight stay, or catching a flight. —Boutayna Chokrane

Gear editor Julian Chokkattu tests dozens of camera bags, and this roll-top model is his all-time favorite. Wandrd's popular Prvke (pronounced "provoke") now has zippered access to the rolltop, a larger side-access opening, and more internal organization. It's plenty roomy and well-sealed against the elements to protect your camera gear. —Scott Gilbertson

The Sony XM4C are finally on sale, and all is right in the world. These are essentially a version two of the cult-classic Sony WH-1000XM4, one of our favorite headphones of 2020, and one of Sony’s best-selling headphones ever. They are really the people’s choice: excellent sound, great noise-canceling (though not as good as Bose’s), a comfortable fit, a folding design, on-ear detection, and decent battery life, all at a reasonable price. —Harry Rabinowitz

With these and the Sony XM4C both at $200 for Black Friday, we’re spoiled for choice. In my review of the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen), my main gripe was price—these are great headphones that float in a strange price point between midrange and premium. That concern flies out the window with this excellent discount. They are supremely comfortable and have some of the best noise-canceling on the market—unmatched at this deal price of $200. —Harry Rabinowitz

The lowest price to date on my favorite pair of wireless earbuds? Sign me up. I lauded the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro in my review because they punch way above their price point, giving much pricier earbuds a run for their money. But it’s call quality that blew me away: I sound better on these earbuds than any other I’ve tested, by far. —Harry Rabinowitz

Finally, a good sale on the Sony WH-1000XM6. This is the lowest price ever for arguably the best noise-canceling headphones you can buy. They go toe-to-toe with Bose for the best noise-canceling around, have a folding, travel-friendly design, and sound absolutely stellar. They set the bar for over-ear headphones, and remain one of the pairs I test others against when writing reviews. —Harry Rabinowitz

Our former top pick for best open earbuds, this pair was replaced only by its successor, the AeroClip 2. It’s also at its lowest price ever (by a lot). These open earbuds wrap around your outer ear, leaving your inner ear open to hear the world around you. They’re comfortable, water- and dust-resistant, and have excellent battery life, meaning you can wear them for outdoor exercise; a rainy dog walk; or anything, really. —Harry Rabinowitz

These are the best ANC earbuds, full stop. They have the strongest automated noise-canceling of any earbuds I’ve tested—New York City streets and busy cafes became a dim hum with ANC on. They also sound great, with clear, detailed instrumentation on some of my favorite albums. —Harry Rabinowitz

This is probably the standout TV deal this Black Friday, if the price holds. The LG C6 has been at its lowest price ever since November started, making it the best OLED TV deal around. We’re still testing it, but early impressions are positive, just like they were for the C5 and C4 before it. —Harry Rabinowitz

Art TVs act as decent televisions plus convincingly realistic wall art, and Samsung’s The Frame is the leader in the category. This 2025 model has an excellent matte, anti-reflective-coated display that makes paintings and wall art look textured and surprisingly realistic. Do note that Samsung only offers 30 free art images—you'll need a $5 monthly subscription to the Samsung Art Store to access the full catalog of over 5,000. —Harry Rabinowitz

One of the best budget TVs at its lowest price ever. Really, getting picture quality that’s this good for under $1,000 is just silly. The TCL QM7L is bright, colorful, and detailed, according to WIRED contributor Rick Broida. Even the built-in speakers ain’t half-bad (though we still recommend getting a soundbar). —Harry Rabinowitz

Another great budget TV at its lowest price ever for Black Friday. Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata highlighted the Hisense U7SG’s very high brightness and clear picture quality, especially for its price point. It comes in two versions: one with Google TV built in and one with Fire TV. (We prefer [and linked to] the Google TV model.) —Harry Rabinowitz

The Roku Pro Series OLED is our favorite budget OLED TV, on sale for the first time ever this Black Friday. It’s one of the lowest-priced OLEDs you can get, and comes with Roku’s easy-to-use operating system (and remote), so it’s a great option for non-techy people looking to try out an OLED screen. The main downside here is that it isn’t as bright as other non-OLED (or pricier OLED) options. —Harry Rabinowitz

Here’s the thing: Like many consumer tech companies, Roku raised prices significantly across its product lines. The Black Friday sale price for the Streaming Stick Plus With Voice Remote—our favorite streaming device for most people—was the same as the previous regular price. You once could have gotten this device for $20. Still, it’s a simple yet fantastic way to access streaming content on your TV, with support for tons of apps and easy navigation. And the current sale price makes it more palatable than the new MSRP. —Les Shu

While it’s a bit long, it’s not very tall, so it’s easy to fit in front of most TVs without blocking them. —Harry Rabinowitz

I used this soundbar for years. It’s one of the best compact, not-too-expensive models you can get. The Gen 2 (along with the Bose TV Speaker [2nd Gen]) is the soundbar I recommend to people who are tight on space and just want something that works. —Harry Rabinowitz

This soundbar plus subwoofer is a fantastic way to upgrade your TV audio system for a reasonable price, especially with this discount. One of our favorite cordless vacuums, the V15 Detect is an oldie but a goodie. It's a great Dyson vacuum that was our top pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still comes with two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). —Nena Farrell

If you want a powerful stick vacuum, you don’t have to spend that much—at least, not on Black Friday. The Shark PowerDetect is a fantastic vacuum that performs just as well (sometimes better!) as more expensive Dyson vacuums in my tests, and it works great for picking up everything you can think of off carpets, rugs, and hard floors alike, though I think it’s best for carpets and rugs. You can get it on sale alone, or bundled with a self-emptying base station that will keep the vacuum charged (well worth the upgrade!) —Nena Farrell

If you’re looking for a new cordless vacuum but want to spend as little as possible (without buying garbage), you’re in luck: Our favorite affordable stick vacuum, the Bissell PowerClean, is on sale, making it even cheaper. It’s a great vacuum that stands upright, has HEPA filtration, and has four lights on the head to help illuminate dust and debris. You’ll get a crevice tool, a small upholstery tool, and a wall mount. —Nena Farrell

The best robot vacuum I've tested is also for sale at one of the best prices I've seen it for. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal is smarter than most vacuums I've tested, thanks to its UV light that helps it find stains around your floors. It does a great job with corner cleaning (nailing my trickiest of corners in my tests) and navigating around my home, though it only can learn a single map, so it's not as ideal for multi-floor homes. But you can just do what my best friend did: buy one for each floor. At this price, you're almost getting it for two for one anyways. —Nena Farrell

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is one of my favorite affordable robot vacuums, especially when it’s on sale, and this is the lowest price you’ll find it for. Roborock’s vacuums have fantastic navigation and an easy-to-use app, and overall do a great job cleaning. The Qrevo 2 Pro especially impressed me with its extendable mop arm, which helps it get under cabinets and clean corners around the house. —Nena Farrell

If you want the cheapest option for a robot vacuum while still getting good quality and mopping, Eufy’s Omni C28 did a great job cleaning multiple floors in my home, making it my overall favorite affordable vacuum pick to this day. For such a well-priced vacuum, it never got lost while navigating my home (a more expensive Eufy vacuum actually did get lost on me, funny enough) and can learn multiple maps if you need to clean more than one floor. It’s often on sale in the $400 range, so this price is the best I’ve seen. —Nena Farrell

This is the automatic litter box I recommend for anyone who wants a super-cheap, self-cleaning option without extra luxe features like a connected app or built-in camera. It has a familiar open-top design that most cats take to easily, and you control its functions with three buttons on the box: clean, refill litter, and power on/off. If you don’t want to break the bank but want to spend less time scooping urine and stool, I recommend this budget model. —Molly Higgins

This automatic litter box has an open, front-facing entrance and sits slightly raised on legs. It connects to Wi-Fi, so you can review your cat’s visits in the phone app. Each entry shows the time, your cat’s weight, and how long the visit lasted. During testing, it was easy to assemble and worked well—we think it’s worth considering, especially at a discount. —Molly Higgins

This pet water fountain is perfect for cats who love drinking from faucets. It features all-stainless-steel construction, which makes it more hygienic and keeps water colder. The tall spigot is great for cats who love long streams of water, and activated carbon filters sit below the steel top. Plus, the top has a reservoir, so water is always available. It's not app-connected, but the small window lets you easily monitor water levels. —Molly Higgins

The Kindle Paperwhite is the best of Amazon’s e-readers to buy thanks to its larger screen and warm front light, plus 16 GB of storage. The cheaper base Kindle doesn’t have any of these and loses an inch of screen space. There’s a new Kindle Paperwhite out as of late October, but only the older model is on sale. Don’t worry—you aren’t missing out on much; I recommend buying the on-sale model over the newest one, since the 12th gen is only two years old and still great. —Nena Farrell

If you want the best e-reader that isn’t a Kindle (and the best-priced colorful e-reader, Kindle or not), the answer is a Kobo, specifically the Kobo Libra Colour. This e-reader has a 7-inch screen, built-in page-turn buttons, and a warm front light, and can be paired with the Kobo stylus so that it doubles as a digital notebook. It had a price hike earlier this year, raising it from $230 to $260, so this price isn’t a great deal compared to what it used to cost, but it’s better to buy it now than pay the new, higher price. —Nena Farrell

So far, this is my favorite deal you can find on a Kindle. I love using a Kindle Scribe as both an e-reader and a digital notebook, especially since it has a nice long battery life and easy-to-use software. I usually recommend the older, second-gen model since it’s cheaper and has most of the same features, but the third-gen Kindle Scribe is now on sale for less than the older one, so it makes sense to upgrade and pay less. My kind of Black Friday deal. —Nena Farrell

If you want the best digital notebook with all the bells and whistles, the ReMarkable Paper Pro is ReMarkable’s colorful and most powerful digital notebook yet. It offers one of the best writing experiences if you want a digital notebook that really feels like writing on paper, with a color screen and a gentle front light. Better yet, the bundle on sale will include the Marker Plus with an eraser and a protective folio. ReMarkable’s devices are rarely on sale, so don’t wait on this deal. —Nena Farrell

If you want a tablet focused on taking notes but not necessarily a digital notebook with an e-paper screen, the TCL Note A1 Nxtpaper is what you’re looking for. It gives you most of what we like about digital notebook devices, with software focused on note-taking, but it still works as an Android tablet so you can stream videos and use it like a regular tablet. —Nena Farrell
