#249. Albania's youth are protesting, no longer leaving the country

Youth protests against a rigid political system and corruption have shaken the government of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama. They also show that fewer young people are willing to emigrate in search of a better future.

In mid-October, students in the Albanian capital Tirana set a suitcase on fire and threw it into the courtyard of the Education Ministry. Everyone in the country understood the symbolism: According to the 2023 census, the population of this Western Balkan country shrunk by about 420,000 between 2011 and 2023 — by nearly 15% — primarily because of emigration.

For a generation of young Albanians, this was the response to a system that gave them little voice. But now young people want to stay, and the protesters are saying that the system has to change.

Known as the "Flamingo Revolution," the social movement began in May with demonstrations against a luxury resort in a coastal reserve that US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner were involved in.

It quickly evolved into broader criticism against corruption, Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and his ruling Socialist Party and the country's entire political class.

Thousands marched almost every evening for four months in protests that were largely peaceful. But on October 13, a student protest escalated and there were clashes with police. Since then, the unrest has continued, with police using tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets against demonstrators. There have been hundreds of arrests and many injuries, amid damage to public and private property.

The protesters have called for Rama's resignation, a transitional government, electoral reform and fresh elections. The movement, which has no leader, has support from people across the political spectrum. And while the prime minister has blamed "foreign hands" for the movement, there seems to be little evidence that external actors are orchestrating the protests, though they may have attempted to exploit the unrest online.

The protesters, who do not feel represented by Albania's democracy, are driven by domestic issues: corruption, the high cost of living and low wages. This is nothing new, but many factors have converged recently: a series of high-level corruption charges, including against ministers and two of Rama's former deputies, rising prices and the fact that Albania is being measured against EU standards by a new generation.

In certain areas, Rama has transformed Albania since taking office in 2013: the economy has grown significantly, as the government likes to point out, and tourism is booming. But the prosperity remains unevenly distributed. Critics accuse the government of channeling too much taxpayer money into a small number of well-connected companies through prestigious projects and public-private partnerships, and in some cases through corrupt business deals, at the expense of healthcare, education and better economic prospects for the wider population.

Rama has rejected the calls for his resignation and has invited protesters to engage in dialogue, which they have so far refused.

In 2008, Rama and Sali Berisha, the long-time chairman of the opposition Democratic Party, worked on a reform to Albania's constitution and electoral law, which was approved by parliament. Since then, it is party leaders who have determined who enters Parliament, which weakens ties between lawmakers and their constituents.

In addition, it has become significantly more difficult for new parties to win seats. In 2025, a new party received about 64,000 votes, but only one seat. The Socialists, by contrast, won about one seat for every 10,000 votes.

Rama has been the leader of the Socialists since 2005, while Berisha first became the chairman of the Democratic Party in 1991. For 21 years, Albania's prime minister has either been Rama or Berisha. Freedom House, a US nongovernmental organization that promotes democracy worldwide, classifies Albania as "partly free" and describes the country's political parties as being "often organized around leading personalities."

Protesters on the streets have said that they want both men to be jailed. Rama has argued that governments should be replaced at the ballot box, not on the streets.

Though the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) acknowledged that parliamentary elections in 2025 were "competitive and professionally managed" it said that they had taken place "in a highly polarized environment and contestants did not enjoy a level playing field."

It added that there were "reports of intimidation, misuse of public resources and pressure on public employees, which undermined equal opportunities."

The Democratic Party also spoke of election fraud and intimidation. Turnout was below 45%.

Many protesters also allege that when it comes to business, what matters is the proximity to people in power. They criticize the public procurement, public auctions and concessions system, which has led to state-owned land, including coastal and protected areas, being sold to private investors.

Ordinary Albanians are feeling the financial brunt. According to the Albanian Institute of Statistics (INSTAT), half of all employees earn less than 60,000 lek (roughly €620 or $680) per month after taxes. But according to Eurostat, food prices are slightly above the EU average and real estate prices in Tirana have nearly doubled since 2018, with rents rising just as quickly.

For many years, young Albanians who were dissatisfied with the system opted to leave the country. The number of Albanian citizens in Germany more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, reaching almost 120,000.

Though it is still too early to say whether there are fewer Albanians leaving today, for many protesters staying has become a political statement.

Rama has argued that his resignation would jeopardize Albania's bid to join the European Union by 2030, but the vast majority of Albanians are pro-European, including those on the streets and in the opposition. From the protesters' perspective, it is the government headed by Rama that is the real obstacle on the path to the EU.

Though there is currently a wave of protests across Europe, the only obvious comparison is with Serbia, where a student-led movement recently forced a long-time ruler from office. Whether Albania will follow this example depends on whether young people, who have traditionally not been deeply engaged in politics, can turn their protests into votes.

What is certain is that for three decades, Albania's leaders have relied on their citizens' suitcases. Now, the country's students have burned that very luggage.

Andi Balla is a doctoral candidate at the Leibniz Institute for East and Southeast European Studies (IOS) in Regensburg, where he is conducting research on demographic debates in Albania. He has written numerous articles on Albania for an international audience.

#247. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#246. A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos

France blames an Iranian cyber unit for sabotaging hundreds of supermarket freezers.

One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.

Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.

The group, which often goes by the online persona CyberAv3ngers, has a history of targeting critical infrastructure. In 2023 and 2024, it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices inside water, manufacturing, and transportation systems across several US states. Operational disruption was minimal, but the attackers left a message each time: “Every equipment ‘made in Israel’ is CyberAv3ngers legal target.”

State-backed Iranian hackers have rarely targeted Europe in this way, however. October’s hacks, experts say, mark an escalation in the Islamic republic’s cyber warfare strategy and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure.

“Iran has very clearly messaged that the global economy will be disrupted as a consequence of it being shut out from the world,” said Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations.

While France and other European countries have largely stayed out of the US and Israel’s campaign against Iran, which started in February, the Islamic republic increasingly views all Nato countries as legitimate targets, she continued. “This is about sowing panic in Europe and increasing that global pain threshold.”

Similar attacks were staged this month against supermarkets in 10 other countries across Europe, though no group has yet been blamed.

Iran has denied any role in the freezer hacks, but France is seeking international arrest warrants for three Iranians allegedly involved: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, believed by US intelligence to be head of the Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command, and two Shahid Kaveh leaders, 37-year-old Mahdi Lashgarian and 35-year-old Reza Salarvand. Both Lashgarians were placed under US sanctions in 2024.

Often staffed with young engineers and software developers, the Revolutionary Guards’ cyber units have developed formidable skills in espionage and cyber warfare.

“Iran is a country of engineers, and people continue to underestimate its capabilities,” said Sanam Vakil, Middle East director at Chatham House think-tank. “It has a long history of successful cyber operations,” she added, noting that Iran had learnt through its own experience of cyber attacks, most notably the Stuxnet assault on its nuclear program by the US and Israel in 2009.

French intelligence agencies have said the group used a Chinese-made scanning tool to scour the public Internet for connected refrigeration units. Infrastructure linked to the group also conducted reconnaissance using Modbus, a digital language widely used to control industrial machinery—a technique Shahid Kaveh has employed since at least April, according to the authorities.

The modus operandi described by the French authorities was consistent with the Iranian attacks in the US in 2023 and 2024, said Cynthia Kaiser, former deputy cyber director at the FBI. Near-identical hacks to those have taken place this year, though CyberAv3ngers did not claim responsibility, and US authorities stopped short of explicitly blaming Iran.

Kaiser said it was also possible that a third state could have contracted Shahid Kaveh to conduct the European attacks. “Even if Iranians were behind the keyboard, these attacks really appear more consistent with Russian-type targeting,” she said. “It wouldn’t surprise me if we eventually uncovered collaboration behind the scenes.”

Russia, like Iran, has sophisticated cyber capabilities and has shown increasing willingness to use them against Europe.

Vakil at Chatham House acknowledged Russian involvement remained a possibility, noting that the strength of the relationship between the two countries was often under-appreciated by Western officials. “Their ties have grown through the context of these wars,” she said, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Iran’s conflict with the US and Israel. In March, Russian state-sponsored hacking group NoName claimed responsibility for a series of attacks on Israeli targets.

Whether or not Shahid Kaveh was working on behalf of Moscow or another power, the operation would have to be sanctioned by the senior leadership of the IRGC, according to Gil Messing, chief of staff at Israeli cyber security group Check Point Software.

Cyber weapons have a limited shelf life, as once a specific software or hardware vulnerability has been exploited, it tends to be almost immediately patched by other potential targets.

“The decision to make such a thing and burn out this capability is something that would have to be authorized by senior levels,” Messing said. “This is not a very sophisticated attack, but it sends a very strong message.”

#245. German Catholic Church abuse victims may receive higher compensation

In a landmark ruling, judges in Cologne found the Catholic Church responsible for abuse committed by clergy members. Victims could now be entitled to more compensation.

The Higher Regional Court of Cologne ruled on Thursday that the Archdiocese of Cologne must pay €550,000 ($603,341) to a now 60-year-old woman. Melanie F.*, the claimant, was subjected to serious sexual abuse by a priest in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

This ruling could result in the Catholic Church paying significantly higher compensation to victims of abuse and sexual violence by priests.

The settlement far exceeds previous sums granted in similar cases. Before this, the highest financial compensation awarded by a court was €300,000. This amount was granted by the Regional Court of Cologne in June 2023 to a former altar boy who was abused by a priest for several years.

Melanie F. was represented by the same lawyer. Since she had already received €360,000 in compensation during previous proceedings, the court granted Melanie F. an additional €190,000.

In determining the appropriate amount of damages, the Seventh Civil Senate of the Higher Regional Court of Cologne pointed to an "abortion performed without the knowledge or consent of the plaintiff, who was only 15 years old at the time" as one of the deciding factors. The judges said that this incident in particular warranted a substantial increase in compensatory damages. The teenager reportedly became pregnant twice during the period of abuse.

Born in 1966, Melanie F. lived in a Catholic orphanage in Bonn in the late 1970s. Bernd U., then a theology student, worked there as a volunteer and cared for several children. After he was ordained as a priest, he took Melanie and a boy two years her senior from the orphanage to live with him.

Beginning in 1979, he subjected the underage Melanie to severe sexual abuse in his residence at the parish. He threatened to send her back to the orphanage if she refused to comply. He subsequently became the legal guardian of both children. Cardinal Joseph Höffner, who was then the Archbishop of Cologne, approved the arrangement.

In its written opinion, the court addressed the question of whether an archdiocese can be held liable for the criminal acts of a member of the clergy. The judges decided to overrule the Cologne Regional Court's ruling from 2023 and gave a detailed explanation of their reasoning. Ultimately, they found that the Church was liable under the principles of official liability.

The Regional Court had previously rejected this argument in 2023, siding with the lawyers of the Archdiocese of Cologne. At the time, the judges ruled that the abuse was not sufficiently linked to Bernd U.'s role as a priest. According to the judges, he had abused his foster child in his capacity as a caregiver, not as part of his priestly duties.

The 2023 ruling was met with disbelief and anger within the Archdiocese of Cologne. The archdiocese was already in turmoil because many Catholics were unhappy with how Cardinal Rainer Maria Woelki handled abuse cases. For decades, Church teachings and statements by Cologne's archbishops had repeatedly emphasized that a priest is a priest in all that he does and cannot simply set that role aside.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But now, the Higher Regional Court of Cologne has concluded that there is in fact a clear connection between Bernd U.'s work for the church and the crimes he committed.

In their decision, they explained that he had assumed a pastoral role in caring for Melanie F. while she was still living in the orphanage and gained her trust through displays of great affection.

His role at the church was described explicitly by the judges as a "cover." It was only much later that he sought to become the children's foster father, a position he would likely not have been able to obtain so easily without the "cover" of being a celibate Catholic priest. In addition, most of the abuse took place in the rectory.

After the ruling, Melanie F. said she was relieved that her years-long legal battle had finally come to an end. But she said she would never be able to put the abuse behind her. "You can't just block it out; you live with it."

The Archdiocese of Cologne said it "respectfully" took note of the decision.

The perpetrator, now 74 years old, was sentenced to 12 years in prison at his 2022 trial. The court found that he had abused nine girls, the youngest of whom was nine years old. The Church subsequently removed him from the priesthood.

"The strategy of the Archdiocese of Cologne to portray its priests' serious sexual crimes as the actions of private individuals has failed miserably," Thomas Schüller, a Catholic canon lawyer, told DW. Schüller described the archdiocese's approach as a "cynical attempt" that betrays the Catholic Church's own understanding of the priestly office.

From now on, the church will be held liable if a priest uses his position to sexually abuse children or teenagers and if the diocese or Protestant regional church has failed to fulfill its supervisory duties adequately.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Schüller said that Germany's Catholic bishops must "significantly increase" compensation payments to survivors. Until now, the bishops had consistently argued that the amounts should be based on current court rulings and legal standards.

However, this ruling will now have "significant financial consequences for both churches," he said, describing the ruling as "a day of hope for many survivors of sexual abuse in both churches."

Matthias Katsch, spokesperson for the survivor advocacy group Eckiger Tisch, also called the ruling "good news."

"Today, it was made clear that the Church must pay for the harm caused by its officials," he said. However, he added that the amount was still too low given the horrific nature of the crimes and their lifelong consequences.

"The Archdiocese of Cologne's leadership turned a blind eye or acted with the grossest negligence," he said, allowing the crimes to happen. Melanie F. had sought compensation of between €800,000 and €900,000.

In March 2026, the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments (UKA), which was established by the German Bishops' Conference in 2021, announced that it had approved payments totaling approximately €93 million for survivors in all dioceses. Since then, several dioceses have published additional studies containing new reports of abuse cases.

Sixteen years after survivors and Jesuit priest Klaus Mertes helped bring the abuse scandal to light, the German Bishops' Conference will now have to prepare for significantly higher compensation payments.

In the United States, where civil lawsuits seeking compensation often involve far higher sums than in Germany, a number of Catholic dioceses have filed for bankruptcy. But that is unlikely to happen in Germany. The Bonn-based law firm of Eberhard Luetjohann, Melanie F.'s attorney, has reported receiving inquiries from hundreds of abuse survivors seeking higher compensation.

Spokesperson for Eckiger Tisch, Matthias Katsch, called on church leaders to engage in dialogue with survivors and their advocacy groups. Katsch said the question of the Church's liability for crimes committed by priests lies at the heart of most cases in which survivors are dissatisfied with the Independent Commission for Recognition Payments' decisions and believe they are entitled to higher compensation.

It is unacceptable, he said, that these survivors must go to court to obtain the compensation they deserve.

This article was originally written in German.

#242. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

So is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from big business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”

#241. Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl

Prior modeling estimated the plume would cover hundreds of square miles.

In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.

The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.

Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.

Lead is a neurotoxin that does not break down in the environment and poses significant health risks, particularly to young children and pregnant people.

In the hours leading to the detonation, the Army released maps showing modeled drift and distribution of the plume. They indicated that airborne lead would travel around 100 miles to the southwest of the facility, while dust deposition would cover around 200 square miles in that direction. Researchers and government workers have already collected air and soil samples from the area, which will act as baseline readings for lead levels in the aftermath and fallout of the detonation.

In preparation for the blast, the Army surrounded the earth-covered containers with sand-and lime fill. They set up water cannons and misters intended to keep dust down. They also covered the top of the container with fire-suppressant foam. The Army documented the efforts with a video posted to social media Wednesday morning.

The explosion follows days of confusion, outrage, questions, and delays. Although the Army said that it has known about the hazardous state of the lead azide since March, Iowans were largely unaware of the situation and the planned detonation until last week. At that time, the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on Friday, November 20. But public alarm and an emergency court filing from environmental groups led to a delay, which was initially scheduled for Monday, then Tuesday, and finally to today.

A federal appeals court initially issued a stay on the Army’s permit to conduct the detonation, and, on Monday, Trump said he ordered the military to halt the operation until the court lifted the stay and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, signed off. Ultimately, the court ruled this week that the Army could move ahead with plans, given no better option.

But questions continue to swirl about how the lead azide got to such a “catastrophically hazardous condition.” On Tuesday, The Washington Post reported that it had viewed emails that suggest the Army knew since at least September 2025, not this past March.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

Topics Amazon Apple Black Friday Gadgets Kitchen

This year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27. While retailers often start featuring their best markdowns on Black Friday itself, there are plenty of early deals worth shopping in the lead-up. Most retailers' official sales do start well before the big day, so shopping strategically ahead of time can save you from missing out on a deal entirely (or dealing with the chaos the day after Thanksgiving).

Cyber Monday takes place on the Monday following Thanksgiving. This year, the shopping event falls on Monday, Nov. 30. While Cyber Monday originally began as an online counterpart to in-person shopping on Black Friday, the two events have merged into an extended online shopping bonanza.

Amazon's Black Friday Week sale kicked off on Nov. 19, which means deals have been live for a week now. Amazon has an incentive to spread out the shopping (to give its delivery drivers a break), so you no longer have to wait until actual Black Friday to save. Deals will continue to go live through Nov. 30.

#238. AI goes from math dunce to genius

It once struggled to get simple sums right. But AI is now tackling tough mathematical problems like the Riemann hypothesis. How AI made this extraordinary leap — and why mathematicians should be "deeply worried."

Last year, I asked ChatGPT to add up my British state pension contributions. Thankfully, I double-checked. The total was wrong by a few pounds.

A friend who teaches math wasn't surprised. Chatbots, he said, often get simple calculations wrong.

Fast-forward to November 2026, and a mathematician working at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, claims to have solved one of the hardest problems in mathematical history with the help of the company's chatbot, Claude.

That problem was the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers, and has baffled mathematicians since 1859.

How did AI go from stumbling over simple arithmetic to scaling such extraordinary mathematical heights?

The answer lies in how AI processes information, said Andrea Asperti, a professor in computer science at Italy's University of Bologna.

Unlike conventional calculators, early chatbots were trained to predict language, producing plausible answers without necessarily doing the math.

Ironically, they may perform millions of calculations to arrive at the wrong answer.

"In a sense, asking why a chatbot makes arithmetic mistakes despite its enormous computational power is like asking why humans make mistakes in mental arithmetic despite having billions of neurons in their brains," Asperti told DW.

Ken Ono, a mathematics professor at the University of Virginia in the United States, recalled how Google's Gemini once concluded that 9.11 was greater than 9.8.

"But make no mistake, those errors are very rare today," Ono told DW.

Asperti attributed AI's gains to gradual improvements in model size, training data and methods rather than a single breakthrough.

AI can now explore different approaches, check its work, correct mistakes and use specialized computational tools.

"What is remarkable is that these relatively incremental technological improvements have resulted in qualitative leaps in intellectual capabilities," Asperti said.

Perhaps most surprising was AI's ability to solve previously unsolved problems — something many had doubted it could do.

"Solving open mathematical problems requires a considerable degree of creativity: it is not simply a matter of retrieving existing knowledge or reproducing known arguments," Asperti said.

Kevin Buzzard, a mathematician at Imperial College London, UK, was excited but not surprised by the proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis.

He had already seen AI resolve a problem in algebraic geometry by finding a counterexample.

"I had thought about the problem myself and could see what the difficulties were. AI cut through them," Buzzard told DW.

Ono draws an analogy with chess: While humans struggle to think several moves ahead, AI can explore countless possibilities. In advanced mathematics, the scope is far greater.

"When it comes to pure mathematics, there are tens of thousands of research papers that are the individual moves that it gets to play with. And what we're seeing is the power of that capacity," Ono said.

Another advantage is AI's ability to recognize connections across different areas of mathematics.

"Most of us become specialists, building upon theories that we learn over time. And it's difficult to become proficient in many more than a small handful of areas," Ono said.

The proposed Riemann proof illustrates that breadth. "It might be 30 or 40 mathematicians you would have to put in a room before you could assemble this proof," he said.

And AI's knowledge extends well beyond math.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ono suggested that the mathematician behind the Claude-assisted proof could have interrupted his work to ask the chatbot: "Hey, by the way, next week I'm going to Hawaii. Come up with a beautiful itinerary for a long weekend in Hawaii."

He and Claude could then have seamlessly returned to advanced mathematics.

"The point I make there is that Claude seems to know everything at a fairly deep level, and humans don't," Ono said.

Ono suggests the individual ideas behind the proposed proof may all be within human intellectual reach.

"But the sheer scope and the ability to assemble ideas that had never been assembled before, that is what is extraordinary here," he said.

Asperti believes AI could develop an entirely different kind of mathematical intuition.

Mathematicians work with abstract spaces of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, which humans, living in a three-dimensional world, struggle to visualize.

AI might develop its own ways of understanding such structures and "discover relationships that are difficult for us even to imagine," Asperti said.

Ono is excited about the future of mathematics but concerned about the future of mathematicians.

Until recently, he would have discouraged young mathematicians from tackling problems like the Riemann hypothesis, saying they could spend 20 years without producing any results.

"Shoot for the moon! The bar has been raised so high that if your primary interest as a mathematician is in the questions themselves, then this is a great time."

"The flip side, if you're a mathematician and your identity is that you want to be the source of the ideas, well, you may have lost most of that."

Ono, who has trained 35 PhD students, is "deeply worried" about their future.

"Make no mistake. In the year 2026, the ground shifted beneath the entire edifice of the world of human mathematical research," he said.

Ono believes the role of future mathematicians will be "much more like being a conductor of the most extraordinary orchestra."

In the past, mathematicians were trained by getting them to prove theorems.

"Now you can prove a theorem by pressing a button," said Buzzard, "so we need new methods."

Buzzard is setting up a lab that emphasizes understanding, explaining and defending complex mathematical arguments.

"The best team for doing mathematics is a computer plus human team, and it is still relatively straightforward to extract insights and understanding from what machines are doing," he said.

But, he said, mathematical research may "end up completely dominated by machines doing things which humans simply cannot comprehend any more, very cheaply and at the touch of a button."

So, that is the issue of solving mathematical problems. What about AI's ability to come up with mathematical problems and propositions, like an Albert Einstein?

Ono said: "If you trained a large language model on all the mathematics and all the physics that was known by the end of the 19th century, would a model spin up Einstein's theory of relativity on its own? I don't think we've seen that sort of creative spark, that sort of ability yet."

#235. Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets

Huawei didn’t try very hard to hide thefts of US trade secrets, DOJ says.

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.

The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its users’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”

As the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of New York Joseph Nocella Jr. said that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage company called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

“The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for Internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology,” the DOJ said.

One of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ said. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ said, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade shows and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The New York Times reported.

Huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ said was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”

Huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the company’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”

Sentencing is scheduled for September 14.

Huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”

Outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by company employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”

Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig said.

After the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.

China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo said.

However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

“This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky said. “No company is too big, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#232. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#231. How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry

When East Germany could no longer afford to import coffee, it introduced a substitute blend containing rye and chicory in 1977. A public outcry ensued. The solution to the problem lay 9,000 kilometers away — in Vietnam.

Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.

That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?

A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.

Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.

However, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin (DDR is the acronym used for East Germany in German). "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices."

The government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes."

In plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.

Even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even said to have exploded.

Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product, and with biting sarcasm, too: "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed."

More than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).

To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's important to recognize coffee's special place in East German society.

"Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," says Wolle.

During the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak."

According to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky.

"Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a big bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.

It is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher.

"Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle says. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care."

Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.

East Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia.

"Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war."

But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam.

"Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," says Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good."

Starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested."

By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past.

"But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," says Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that."

There’s no mention of it on the packages — and if there is, it’s in microscopic print.

"The Vietnamese don’t make a big deal out of their role because they themselves probably still believe that coffee has to come from Brazil — or at least from Latin America — to be any good," says Wolle.

Passionate coffee drinkers may not care where the hot beverage comes from — as long as it doesn't taste like spelt and sugar beets, as the much-maligned East German Kaffee Mix once did.

This article was originally written in German.

#230. Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop

Militaries have many reasons to target data centers and the cloud in wartime.

Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion.

In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine:

We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

Jarnecki also highlighted the fact that relatively cheap kamikaze drones can inflict disproportionate economic costs and create widespread cloud disruptions when striking data centers:

The second reason that we’ve seen targeting particularly in Russia’s largest data centers or some of Russia’s largest public cloud data centers like Yandex, as well as American hyperscalers that are based in the Gulf, is to impose economic cost in a way that would be disadvantageous for an adversary and would otherwise be quite difficult to impose in other ways. So it’s relatively low cost of munition to high cost of disruption. If you think about the amount of investment that’s been put forward by AWS and other companies in the Gulf to build out these data center installations relative to the cost of the amount of Shahed drones that are manufactured, produced, and utilized by Iran to target these data centers, I would put it very, very conservatively at 100X or even more. The cost ratio is really very lucrative for the adversary, and it provides the opportunity to really degrade the economic outcomes of who you are targeting.

Much of the discussion also focused on cloud resilience lessons for both governments and hyperscalers, with the latter including large cloud and data center operators such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta. Jarnecki highlighted the example of how Ukraine took steps to safeguard its cloud infrastructure when Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian military forces to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022:

I think that Ukraine anticipated this problem set very effectively. They anticipated and understood that Russia would not be discriminating necessarily in its targeting of civilian digital infrastructure particularly, and therefore conducted a large-scale cloud migration at the onset of the full-scale war in part in reaction to the anticipated targeting but then also actual targeting that took place through kinetic means.

Such lessons are important because 2026 is unlikely to be the last year in which data centers come under substantial military attack, Jarnecki said:

Unfortunately, I think that this really does indicate a continuation of this kind of targeting, not just because data centers are, despite efforts to harden some of them, relatively squishy, relatively easy to find, and have the potential, because of their complexity, to induce cascading risks within the facility or more widely if they are hit particularly by kinetic munitions. So at present, I would say it’s a dangerous trend that is likely to crop up again.

Throughout the event, Jarnecki also addressed viewer questions about whether data centers can realistically be hardened or built underground to withstand physical attacks, and even how orbital data centers or low-Earth orbit satellite constellations such as Starlink could provide backup options from space.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#228. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#225. Russia sports ban: Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback

As European countries challenge Russia's sporting return, Ukrainian Olympian Vladyslav Heraskevych believes the IOC is facing a "very big crisis."

Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.

Heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport. He made headlines at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina when he was disqualified for his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed in the war with Russia.

On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.

"Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities," she said.

In an interview with DW, Heraskevych described the EU move as coming "better late than never."

"We waited a long time for this backlash," he said at the International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation World Cup in Altenberg, Germany, his first competition since the Winter Olympics.

"I'm really happy to see that people start to care about sports and they understand the value of sports as a huge platform," he added.

In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) paved the way for Russia's full return to international sport by ending its recommendation that Russian athletes be allowed to compete as neutrals, without their flag, colors or anthems. The IOC also said Russian teams should be allowed to return to international competition.

Several major Olympic sports, such as swimming and gymnastics, have already fully reinstated Russia, despite the country's ongoing attacks on Ukraine.

"It makes no sense to me," Heraskevych said.

However, in recent weeks there has been a growing European pushback against the easing of Russia's sporting isolation.

Among the catalysts was a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn a ban on Russia in international ice hockey. That prompted seven European countries to say they would refuse to play against Russia, while Germany, at one point, said withdrawing as host of next year's men's world championship was an option.

The dispute over the CAS ruling drew a response from the Kremlin.

"It is a flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter [the IOC's rulebook] and leads toward the destruction of Olympism as a whole," Russian President Vladimir Putin said in China last week.

"Sport, like art, should bring people together."

Meanwhile, a group of Nordic and Baltic countries want the EU to go even further, pushing for an immediate EU-wide visa ban on all Russian athletes.

"The matter is too urgent to wait until [new visa rules] enter into force," the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden wrote in a November 23 letter to von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.

"From my perspective, the IOC is in a very big crisis," Heraskevych said, referencing the European pushback.

Blanket bans could have a huge effect on qualifying events in Europe for the 2028 Los Angeles Summer Olympics.

Under its president, Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has sought to bring Russia, an Olympic powerhouse, back in from the cold. Coventry has argued that athletes shouldn't be punished for the actions of their governments, and the IOC has strengthened its political neutrality rules in the Olympic Charter.

However, Heraskevych takes exception to the idea that sport should be kept out of politics.

"We are not living in a bubble," he said.

"Already more than 800 people who were part of the sport family in Ukraine were killed. Ukrainian hockey stadiums, Ukrainian swimming pools, anything related to sports have also been attacked. So we cannot separate sport and politics in Ukraine. The same way Russian sport is involved in politics."

Critics have accused Coventry of cozying up to Russia. In September, it emerged that she had written a letter to Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's sports minister and president of the Russian Olympic Committee, wishing him luck ahead of an international sports forum.

Degtyarev has been sanctioned by the EU. The IOC has declined to comment on the letter but not denied its existence.

Heraskevych said he was not "angry" with any particular Russian athlete, and even floated the idea of a team of Russian refugees.

"I am not against peaceful athletes competing," he said.

"They should be part of competition only if they are part of a refugee team. So, if they have refugee status in another country, and if they condemn the war that Russia started in Ukraine."

#224. Etsy clarifies AI terms after seller backlash

One veteran illustrator dismisses revisions as “sugar coating.”

After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.

In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”

“Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”

Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the company had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”

He said he still plans on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.

“I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he said. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”

He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

“This is the worst two-to-three weeks out of the year to do this, bar none,” he said.

The fracas began earlier this month, when the company first proposed new contractual language. The updated terms read:

As a result, a slew of vendors pulled up stakes, with some saying they had “burned their Etsy shop to the ground” or that they “just killed our Etsy store after 13 years.”

Etsy’s change is reminiscent of a recent dust-up involving Meta, where the tech giant had wanted to “require Meta Business account users to allow extensive AI training on external websites linked on Facebook.” Meta then indefinitely paused that move.

Last month, Etsy also told sellers that it would “set clearer restrictions on AI use,” despite the fact that AI-generated items remain for sale all over the site.

“Today, many active buyers say they can’t tell which items involve AI-generated content,” James Ossman, the company’s vice president of customer operations, wrote on October 22. “It’s become a top-three barrier to shopping more often on Etsy.”

For years, Etsy has been notoriously poor at enforcing its own rules, not only regarding AI but also the official prohibitions on selling sex toys, pornography, and even purported witchcraft spells.
